title: Is LeetCode Dead? What's the Alternative?
author: Gregor Ojstersek
summary: Gregor Ojstersek, drawing on conversations with engineers, hiring managers and recruiters, asks whether LeetCode-style technical interviews are on the way out. His answer is that they are declining but not dead: Big Tech and other large companies still use them for objectivity at high applicant volume, while small and mid-size companies and AI labs increasingly do not. He notes that such interviews measure practice at puzzle patterns more than the skills a job needs, and that AI can now solve them in seconds. Emerging alternatives include code review exercises (including Google's Code Comprehension round), product and technical deep dives, and pair programming with AI allowed. For his own recommendations he favors open-ended questions about real projects, job-relevant pair programming, or a mix, judging candidates on their reasoning, trade-offs, communication and whether they verify AI output. He advises against take-home tasks because AI makes the resulting signal weak.
points: LeetCode-style interviews reward preparation on puzzle patterns and often tell an interviewer little about day-to-day engineering skill.
Usage is declining but persists at Big Tech, where high applicant volume favors an objective measure, so candidates targeting those firms should still practice.
Code review exercises and Google's Code Comprehension round test how candidates read unfamiliar code, find problems and communicate trade-offs, which mirrors real work.
Ojstersek recommends open-ended project discussions and job-relevant pair programming that allow AI, judging judgment and validation of output over the final code.
Take-home tasks give a weak signal because AI can generate a polished solution without the candidate understanding it.
quotes: So, basically, with the leetcode-style type of interview, you don’t really assess the actual skills that a specific engineer needs to be able to do the job well. You assess whether the person has been practicing such types of challenges or not.
And if the standard in our industry is AI-assisted engineering, then it really makes no sense to “check the tech skills” with problems, which can be easily solved with a prompt.
In this round, you are evaluating how well candidates understand unfamiliar code, identify potential problems, communicate feedback, and make trade-offs.

The key is to understand their judgment. How they approach solving problems, what alternatives they have thought of, whether they are a team player, and of course, how they have used AI or would use it to help them deliver the project faster.
The key to this challenge is not the end solution and how the code looks in the end, but how it feels working with them, and how good their judgment is in general.
Leetcode is not dead, but I believe the actual usage is declining and is used mostly in bigger companies, due to the high volume of applicants.
The take-home task is something that I believe to be less relevant these days, as basically anyone can generate the solution based on requirements and push it to a public repo on GitHub.
